title: Coding with AI without creating technical debt
summary: AI coding assistants save real time, as long as everyone knows who is accountable for what. Roles, a lightweight spec-driven method, shorter iterations and a one-minute daily demo instead of the stand-up.
body:
Agentic coding tools (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor) have changed the way I work. Used well, they save a considerable amount of time. Used badly, they produce invisible technical debt that you pay back, with interest, a few months later. How can you stay in control of code that nobody really wrote?

In this article we won't compare tools or go through their configuration; we'll look at the organisation around them: who is accountable for what, the specification method I apply on my engagements, and what AI changes in our agile rituals.

## AI carries no responsibility

A coding assistant proposes; it doesn't decide. When a generated line reaches production, someone accepted it, and that person answers for it, not the tool. On my engagements, I set out responsibilities on day one:

- **The product owner** owns the need: they approve the specification before a single line is written;
- **The developer** owns the code: they review every diff as they would a colleague's and can explain every line they merge;
- **The reviewer** owns quality: a pull request produced by an agent goes through the same review as any other, no more, no less;
- **The assistant** executes: on a well-scoped task, within defined permissions, following written conventions (`CLAUDE.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`).

The rule is simple: if nobody can explain a piece of code, it doesn't ship.

## A tailored SDD method

Spec-Driven Development (SDD) means writing the specification before the code and giving it to the agent as the source of truth. GitHub Spec Kit offers a complete framework; on my engagements I use a lighter version, sized for the team and the .NET stack:

1. **The specification**: one page, no more. The need, the business rules, the edge cases and the acceptance criteria, written with the product owner;
2. **The red test**: before any implementation, we write the tests that express the acceptance criteria. They must fail;
3. **The implementation**: the agent works on a dedicated branch with a single goal, making the tests pass, within the project's conventions;
4. **The refactoring**: once the tests are green, we clean up, simplify and delete what isn't needed;
5. **The review**: one topic per pull request, reviewed by a human before merging.

```text
specification → tests (red) → implementation (green) → refactoring → pull request
```

Why the test before the code? Because an agent is very good at writing tests that validate what it has just produced, mistakes included. A test written upfront validates the need instead.

## Agile: more iterations, shorter ones

AI doesn't change the principles of agility; it changes the pace. When implementation gets cheaper, what becomes scarce is user feedback. Rather than two-week sprints that ship a lot at once, I favour short iterations: one specification, one feature, one demo.

You correct course earlier, before the agent has built three floors on a bad foundation.

## No stand-up: one minute of demo

On my engagements, I replaced the daily stand-up with a one-minute demo per person per day. No "yesterday I did, today I will": you show what works, on screen, in the test environment.

Why? Because with an agent it is easy to produce a lot of code without finishing anything. The demo forces you to deliver something that works, every day. Anything you can't show in one minute is either too big, so we split it, or blocked, so we discuss it right afterwards with only the people involved.

## Technical debt, the hidden cost

Technical debt produced with AI doesn't show straight away. The code compiles, the tests pass, the feature works. A few months later you discover three different implementations of the same service, needless abstractions and dependencies nobody chose.

The guardrails I apply every time:

- **Written conventions**: architecture, naming, security. What isn't written down doesn't exist for the agent;
- **Automated checks**: build, tests, static analysis and a performance budget on every pull request, so debt shows up immediately;
- **Short pull requests**: a two-thousand-line diff doesn't get reviewed, it gets skimmed;
- **Time to delete**: every iteration sets aside some clean-up, otherwise nobody does it.

## Conclusion

AI saves real time, as long as you never delegate judgement to it. Clear responsibilities, a specification before the code, short iterations and a one-minute daily demo: nothing revolutionary, but it is what separates a team that speeds up from a team that goes into debt.

title: Sovereign cloud: hosting in Europe without sacrificing the experience
summary: Azure isn't the only way to host in Europe. A tour of sovereign hosts, and how to choose the one that fits your project.
body:
"Hosting in Europe" has become a concrete requirement for many of my clients: GDPR compliance, sensitive data, or simply a sovereignty choice. The good news is you no longer have to choose between sovereignty and deployment comfort.

## Azure when the ecosystem justifies it

For a platform already invested in the Microsoft ecosystem (Entra ID, Service Bus, Functions), Azure remains coherent and powerful. European regions cover most data-residency needs.

## European sovereign hosts have grown up

- **Clever Cloud** (France, SecNumCloud/HDS certified): managed PaaS, first-class PostgreSQL and Redis, git-push deploys. Ideal for a cost-controlled SaaS that wants to stay 100% European.
- **Infomaniak** (Switzerland): managed Kubernetes and object storage, perfect when the positioning (luxury, health) demands Swiss residency.

## The deciding factor

It isn't cloud dogma, it's context: business model, regulatory constraints, team skills. The key is to keep the boundaries (storage, database, observability) behind replaceable interfaces, so you're never locked into one provider.

Unsure which hosting fits your project best? That's exactly the kind of scoping I do at the start of an engagement.
